transcription.tex: 18 A circle has equation \((x-1)^2+y^2=k\), where \(k>0\).\par The straight line \(L\) with equation \(y=ax\) cuts the circle at two distinct points.\par Prove that \(k>\dfrac{a^2}{1+a^2}\).

transcription.tex: Substituting \(y=ax\) into \((x-1)^2+y^2=k\):\[\begin{aligned}(x-1)^2+a^2x^2&=k\\x^2-2x+1+a^2x^2-k&=0\\x^2(1+a^2)-2x+1-k&=0\end{aligned}\]The straight line cuts the circle at two distinct points, so this equation has two distinct real roots, so\[\begin{aligned}b^2-4ac&>0\\(-2)^2-4(1+a^2)(1-k)&>0\\4-4(1-k+a^2-ka^2)&>0\\4k-4a^2+4ka^2&>0\\-a^2+k+ka^2&>0\\-a^2+k(1+a^2)&>0\\k&>\frac{a^2}{1+a^2}\end{aligned}\]

transcription.tex: As \(a\) is positive, multiplying both sides by \(a\) does not reverse the inequality.\par So \(a^2+1\ge2a\).\par Then \(a^2-2a+1\ge0\).\par Factorising gives\par \((a-1)^2\ge0\) which we know is true.
transcription.notes: Visually transcribed original text and mathematics.

transcription.tex: \textbf{a} By squaring both sides, consider \((p+q)^2\).\[\begin{aligned}(p+q)^2&=p^2+2pq+q^2\\&=(p-q)^2+4pq\end{aligned}\]\((p-q)^2\ge0\) since it is a square, so \((p+q)^2\ge4pq\).\par \(p\) and \(q\) are both positive, so \(p>0\) and \(q>0\). Therefore, \(p+q>0\).\par So \(p+q\ge\sqrt{4pq}\).
